client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next month, and I honestly don't know how I'm going to get through them. Statistics has been a nightmare all semester — I've been struggling to keep up, and now it feels like everything is piling on at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still going to be there no matter what we discuss here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the pressure of exams, the struggle with Statistics, and maybe even some doubt about whether reaching out for support is worth it. That last part stands out to me, and I want to gently acknowledge it: it takes courage to show up even when part of you isn't sure it'll help. What would it mean for you if talking things through *could* make even a small difference in how you approach the next few weeks?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess if it actually helped, it would mean I'd feel less like I'm drowning every time I open my Statistics textbook. But honestly, I'm not sure talking about it changes the fact that I don't understand the material and I'm running out of time. It's hard to feel hopeful when the problem feels so concrete and real, you know?
therapist: That image of drowning every time you open the textbook is really powerful — it tells me this isn't just about the material itself, but about how overwhelming and maybe even hopeless it *feels* in those moments. You're right that talking won't magically teach you Statistics, but I'm curious: when you sit down with that textbook, what's the very first thought that goes through your mind before you've even read a single word?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, the first thought is usually something like "you're already behind, this is pointless." It just hits me immediately, before I've even done anything wrong yet, and then I feel this wave of guilt like I should have started sooner or studied harder weeks ago. It's like I've already failed in my head before I've even tried.
therapist: What you just described — "already failed before you've even tried" — that's a really important pattern to notice, and it has a name in CBT: it's called a automatic negative thought, and it's acting like a bully that shows up *before* you even have a chance to prove it wrong. That wave of guilt and the rush of "what's the point" makes so much sense given how long that voice has been beating you up. What do you think would happen if, just for an experiment, you opened the textbook and gave yourself permission to only understand *one small thing* — not catch up, not fix everything, just one thing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but I'm not sure one small thing is going to feel like enough when I think about how much ground I need to cover. I'm worried that if I only let myself do a little, I'll use it as an excuse to stop, and then I'll feel even more guilty for not doing more. It's like I can't win either way — if I do too little I feel lazy, and if I try to do everything I feel overwhelmed.
therapist: You've just described a trap that's exhausting to live in — where both doing a little *and* doing a lot feel like losing, which means your mind has set up a situation where you can't give yourself credit no matter what you do. I notice there's a real urgency in how you're describing this, like the anxiety is right there at the surface even as we talk. Can we slow down for just a second and look at that rule your mind has created — where does that voice that calls you "lazy" for doing a little actually come from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think that voice probably comes from my parents, honestly — they always had really high expectations and "good enough" was never really a thing in our house. But I don't know if digging into where it comes from actually helps me study better for next month, like does understanding the origin of the voice make it quieter? I guess I'm just not sure how going back there connects to getting through my exams.
therapist: That's such a fair and practical question, and I want to honor it — you're not here to just explore the past, you're here because exams are real and coming fast. But here's the connection: that voice your parents' expectations built is the exact same one saying "you're already behind, this is pointless" before you've opened a single page, and *that* voice is what's making studying harder, not just the Statistics itself. So understanding it isn't about going back — it's about loosening its grip so it stops stealing your focus every time you sit down to work.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, when you put it that way, I can kind of see the connection — like the voice isn't just background noise, it's actually getting in the way of me sitting down and focusing. But I guess I'm skeptical about how quickly that grip can loosen, because I've had that voice my whole life and exams are in a month, not a year. Is there something more immediate I can actually do when that thought hits me mid-study session?
therapist: Yes, absolutely — and this is where CBT gets really practical and concrete. When that "you're already behind, this is pointless" thought hits mid-session, try this: pause, name it out loud or on paper ("there's that voice again"), and then ask it one simple question — "what's the actual evidence that *this* moment of studying is pointless?" That small act of stepping back and questioning the thought, rather than just absorbing it as truth, is something you can practice starting tonight.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I like that it's something concrete I can actually do, but I'm a little worried that in the moment, when the anxiety is really high, I'm just going to forget to do it or it's going to feel forced and weird. Like, I can imagine myself sitting there stressed out and the idea of stopping to write down "there's that voice again" just feeling kind of ridiculous. What if the anxiety is just too loud to actually pause like that?
therapist: That worry makes complete sense, and honestly it's a sign you're thinking about this realistically rather than just hoping it'll magically work. The good news is that the technique doesn't have to look perfect — even just muttering "there's that voice" under your breath counts, and the more you practice it in low-stakes moments, the more automatic it becomes before the high-anxiety ones hit. Would it help to actually try it out a few times this week when the stress is more manageable, so it feels less foreign when things get intense?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I could try it in lower-stress moments, that does make it feel a little less daunting. But I'm realizing that even outside of studying, I'm kind of always on edge about the exams — like there isn't really a "low-stress" moment in my day right now because it's always sitting in the back of my mind. Does it still count as practice if I'm already pretty anxious when I try it?
therapist: Yes, it absolutely still counts — in fact, practicing when you're already a bit anxious is actually closer to the real conditions you're training for, so it's not a setback, it's just a slightly harder level. What you're describing though — that constant background hum of exam anxiety that never really switches off — sounds genuinely exhausting, like your nervous system never gets a break. Are there any moments in your day, even tiny ones like making a cup of tea or walking somewhere, where you could intentionally give your brain a five-minute "off duty" signal?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: There are moments like that, I guess — I usually walk to campus in the morning and sometimes I make tea before bed. But even in those moments, my brain just kind of automatically drifts back to the exams, like I'll be walking and suddenly I'm mentally rehearsing everything I don't know yet. I'm not sure I actually know how to tell my brain to be "off duty" when it seems determined to stay on.
therapist: It's really common for an anxious brain to hijack those quiet moments — it genuinely thinks it's helping you by keeping the threat front and center, even when it's actually just wearing you out. The walk and the tea are perfect starting points though, not because you'll perfectly clear your mind, but because you can gently practice noticing when it drifts and just redirecting your attention back to what you can actually sense — the feel of the ground, the warmth of the mug — even for thirty seconds at a time. What do you think it would feel like to give yourself permission to let the exams wait for just that one small window?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, even imagining letting the exams wait for a few minutes makes me feel a little anxious, like I'd be doing something wrong or irresponsible. I think part of me genuinely believes that if I stop thinking about them even briefly, I'll fall further behind somehow, even though logically I know that doesn't really make sense. It's like my brain has convinced me that the worrying itself is productive, even when it's just exhausting me.
therapist: You've just identified something really profound — that the worrying *feels* like doing something, like a form of control, even when it's actually draining the energy you need to actually study. And yet the way you're saying this feels almost quiet and resigned, like part of you already knows this truth but hasn't quite been able to act on it yet. What would it mean for you to consider that resting your mind for a few minutes isn't falling behind — it's actually part of how you get through this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
